<hypothesis>
kind: hypothesis
title: Target-Model-Guided Prompt Compression via Attention Saliency
hypothesis: >-
  Using the target LLM's own attention-saliency maps or gradient-based input attribution (e.g., integrated gradients, attention
  rollout) to select which prompt tokens to retain will outperform proxy-model-based compression (LLMLingua, LongLLMLingua,
  LLMLingua-2) because it directly captures what the target model actually uses for generation, rather than what a small proxy
  model thinks is important.
motivation: >-
  All existing prompt compression methods (LLMLingua, LongLLMLingua, LLMLingua-2, Selective-Context, PCRL, Perception Compressor)
  use a SMALL PROXY MODEL (GPT-2, LLaMA-7B, BERT, etc.) to estimate token importance. This creates a distribution mismatch:
  the proxy model's notion of 'important tokens' may not match what the actual target LLM attends to during generation. By
  using the target model's own attention or gradient-based saliency, we directly measure what the target model uses, eliminating
  the proxy gap. This is especially impactful for open models (LLaMA, Mistral, Qwen) where we have full white-box access to
  attention maps.
assumptions:
- >-
  The target LLM's attention patterns or input gradients correlate with token importance for the downstream task
- >-
  White-box access to the target model is available (open-weight models like LLaMA, Mistral, Qwen)
- >-
  Attention-saliency can be computed efficiently (single forward pass or few backward passes) relative to the compression
  budget
- >-
  The target model's attention on the prompt tokens is stable across similar prompts/tasks (enabling caching or reuse)
investigation_approach: >-
  Implement a tiny experiment comparing three compression strategies on LongBench (single-doc QA, multi-doc QA, summarization)
  using LLaMA-3-8B as the target model: (1) LLMLingua (GPT-2 perplexity baseline), (2) LongLLMLingua (query-aware contrastive
  perplexity), (3) Target-Model-Guided: compute attention rollout or integrated gradients from the target model on a calibration
  set, use mean attention-to-prompt or gradient magnitude per token as importance score, compress by retaining top-k tokens.
  Measure F1/ROUGE vs compression ratio. Total compute: <1 GPU-hour on a single A100/H100.
success_criteria: >-
  Target-model-guided compression achieves higher task performance (F1 for QA, ROUGE for summarization) than LLMLingua and
  LongLLMLingua at the same compression ratios (2x, 4x, 8x) on at least 2 of 3 LongBench task categories. A null result (no
  improvement) would still be informative—it would suggest the proxy models already capture the target model's token importance
  well, or that attention-saliency is not the right signal.
related_works:
- >-
  LLMLingua (Jiang et al., EMNLP 2023): Uses GPT-2/LLaMA-7B perplexity as proxy for token importance. Fundamentally differs
  by using a small proxy model instead of the target model's own attention.
- >-
  LongLLMLingua (Jiang et al., ACL 2024): Adds query-awareness via contrastive perplexity (perplexity shift when conditioned
  on question). Still uses a proxy model (LLaMA-7B) for all importance estimates.
- >-
  LLMLingua-2 (Pan et al., ACL Findings 2024): Trains a BERT-based token classifier on GPT-4 distilled data. Task-agnostic,
  uses bidirectional context but still a proxy model (XLM-RoBERTa/mBERT), not the target LLM.
- >-
  Selective-Context (Li et al., 2023): Uses self-information from a small LM. Proxy-based, no query awareness.
- >-
  PCRL (Jung & Kim, 2023): RL-based discrete compression with ROUGE reward. Trains a policy on a small model (DistilBERT),
  not the target LLM.
- >-
  Perception Compressor (Tang et al., NAACL 2025): Training-free, uses guiding questions and contrast perplexity from a small
  LM. Still proxy-based.
- >-
  Attention-based KV cache compression (e.g., Keyformer, PyramidInfer): Uses target model attention to drop KV cache entries
  DURING generation, not for prompt compression BEFORE generation. Different problem setting.
inspiration: >-
  Cross-domain transfer from mechanistic interpretability (attribution patching, activation patching) and model compression
  (attention-guided pruning). In mechanistic interpretability, we routinely use the target model's own attention/activations
  to understand its behavior. In model compression (e.g., MiniLMv2, attention distillation), we use teacher model attention
  to guide student training. The novel move is applying target-model attention/attribution to PROMPT COMPRESSION (selecting
  input tokens) rather than model compression (selecting weights/heads) or KV cache compression (selecting past keys/values).
  This connects the interpretability insight 'the model tells you what it attends to' with the prompt compression problem
  'which input tokens matter'.
terms:
- term: Proxy model
  definition: >-
    A smaller, faster model (e.g., GPT-2, LLaMA-7B, BERT) used to estimate token importance for compressing prompts intended
    for a larger target LLM
- term: Target model
  definition: >-
    The actual LLM that will process the compressed prompt at inference time (e.g., LLaMA-3-8B, Mistral-7B, GPT-4)
- term: Attention rollout
  definition: >-
    A method to compute token-to-token attribution by recursively multiplying attention matrices across layers, showing how
    much each input token contributes to each output token
- term: Integrated gradients
  definition: >-
    A gradient-based attribution method that integrates gradients along a straight-line path from a baseline input to the
    actual input, providing token-level importance scores
- term: Attention-saliency map
  definition: >-
    A per-token importance score derived from the target model's attention patterns, e.g., mean attention received by each
    prompt token across heads and layers
- term: Contrastive perplexity
  definition: >-
    LongLLMLingua's metric: perplexity(token | context) - perplexity(token | question, context), measuring how much the question
    reduces uncertainty about a token
summary: >-
  Current prompt compression methods all rely on small proxy models to decide which tokens to keep. This hypothesis proposes
  using the target LLM's own attention-saliency or gradient-based input attribution directly—measuring what the target model
  actually attends to—eliminating the proxy gap. Tiny experiments on LongBench with LLaMA-3-8B can validate this in <1 GPU-hour.
alternates:
- title: Calibration-Set Attention Distillation
  hypothesis: >-
    Instead of computing attention per-query, pre-compute a universal token-importance profile for the target model on a small
    calibration set (e.g., 100 diverse prompts), then use this static profile for all future compressions. This amortizes
    the white-box cost and tests whether the target model has consistent attention patterns across tasks.
  why_it_could_win: >-
    If the target model's attention-to-prompt-tokens is relatively stable across tasks (e.g., always attends to instructions,
    entity names, question words), a one-time calibration suffices. This would be dramatically faster than per-query attribution
    and more practical for production. It beats the main hypothesis if per-query computation is the bottleneck and attention
    patterns are task-invariant.
- title: Hybrid Proxy-Target Compression
  hypothesis: >-
    Use the proxy model (e.g., LLMLingua-2) for coarse-grained document/sentence selection (cheap, fast), then apply target-model
    attention-saliency only for fine-grained token selection within the retained segments. This combines the efficiency of
    proxy models with the accuracy of target-model guidance.
  why_it_could_win: >-
    Pure target-model attribution on 10k-token prompts may be slow. Coarse proxy filtering reduces the token budget for expensive
    target-model attribution. This beats the main hypothesis if the compute budget is tight and coarse proxy decisions are
    already near-optimal, leaving only fine-grained selection to benefit from target-model signals.
- title: Gradient-Free Attention Sinks for Black-Box Target Models
  hypothesis: >-
    For API-only target models (no white-box access), use the 'attention sink' phenomenon (first few tokens accumulate disproportionate
    attention) as a proxy for the target model's internal attention: retain tokens that would become attention sinks (early
    instruction tokens, question tokens) and use a small proxy model for the rest.
  why_it_could_win: >-
    The main hypothesis requires white-box access. If the attention sink pattern is universal and predictable, we can approximate
    target-model attention without access. This beats the main hypothesis in black-box settings (OpenAI API, Anthropic API)
    where the main hypothesis is inapplicable. It wins if attention sinks reliably indicate target-model importance across
    diverse prompts.
_relation_rationale: >-
  Same conceptual frame; defects in experimental pipeline prevent any evidence from bearing on the claim.

id: experiment_iter2_dir1
type: experiment
objective: >-
  Run the complete wide-screen experiment on the real LongBench mini-split (450 examples, 50 per task × 9 tasks) with LLaMA-3-8B
  4-bit quantized as target model, comparing all 7 compression methods + baseline at 2x/4x/8x compression ratios. Fix all
  Iteration 1 bugs: LLMLingua rate parameter (convert ratios 2x/4x/8x → rates 0.5/0.25/0.125), calibration profile building,
  float-to-int conversion, synthetic data fallback, MINI_SPLIT_SIZE=50. Output per-example metrics (F1, ROUGE-L) AND full
  statistical analysis: bootstrap 95% CIs (1000 resamples) for all method×category×ratio cells, paired bootstrap significance
  tests (Attention Rollout vs each proxy baseline and vs Baseline), validated pre-registered rank-based selection protocol,
  corrected rank tables with real distributions.
approach: >-
  Modify the existing method.py from art_nzZ_rM-e6Rwh: (1) Load LLaMA-3-8B with 4-bit quantization (bitsandbytes) on A100/H100;
  (2) Use real LongBench mini-split from art_5_Iw7LOgL61k (processed_data/mini_data_out.json); (3) Fix LLMLingua rate parameter:
  compression_ratio → rate = 1/ratio; (4) Fix calibration profile: pre-compute attention rollout on 20 diverse calibration
  prompts from the holdout split, average per-position importance; (5) Fix integer conversion: ensure all token counts and
  indices are int; (6) Implement all 7 methods: LLMLingua, LongLLMLingua, LLMLingua-2, Attention Rollout (per-query), Calibration
  Distilled, Hybrid (LLMLingua-2 coarse 2x → attention fine), Attention Sink (first-k + proxy); (7) Run full 450 × 8 × 3 =
  10,800 evaluations; (8) Compute bootstrap confidence intervals and paired significance tests inline; (9) Validate ranking
  protocol: rank by (F1+ROUGE-L)/2 per (category, ratio), average across 9 cells; (10) Output method_out.json with per-example
  results AND aggregate statistics tables for direct paper inclusion.

title: Three Recent Prompt Compression Methods
summary: >-
  The research focuses on three recent prompt compression methods for LLM inference: LLMLingua-2 (token-classifier distillation),
  LongLLMLingua (query-aware contrastive perplexity), and Selective Context (information-theoretic token filtering). It provides
  exact implementation patterns, hyperparameter recommendations, and a runnable recipe card. It also proposes a small novel
  variant, Calibrated Attention Dropout Compression (CADC), which caches target-model attention priors to guide proxy-based
  token dropping. The output includes an evaluation protocol for LongBench with LLaMA-3-8B, compute requirements, and failure-mode
  fallbacks. Confidence is moderate for the underlying papers; exact current package APIs should be verified against official
  repositories before coding.

We use a max encoder step of 750 for the audio input, based on the implementation choices presented in BIBREF30 and 128 for the text input because it covers the maximum length of the transcripts. The vocabulary size of the dataset is 3,747, including the “_UNK_\" token, which represents unknown words, and the “_PAD_\" token, which is used to indicate padding information added while preparing mini-batch data. The number of hidden units and the number of layers in the RNN for each model (ARE, TRE, MDRE and MDREA) are selected based on extensive hyperparameter search experiments. The weights of the hidden units are initialized using orthogonal weights BIBREF31 ], and the text embedding layer is initialized from pretrained word-embedding vectors BIBREF32 .\nIn preparing the textual dataset, we first use the released transcripts of the IEMOCAP dataset for simplicity. To investigate the practical performance, we then process all of the IEMOCAP audio data using an ASR system (the Google Cloud Speech API) and retrieve the transcripts. The performance of the Google ASR system is reflected by its word error rate (WER) of 5.53%.\nPerformance evaluation\nAs the dataset is not explicitly split beforehand into training, development, and testing sets, we perform 5-fold cross validation to determine the overall performance of the model. The data in each fold are split into training, development, and testing datasets (8:0.5:1.5, respectively). After training the model, we measure the weighted average precision (WAP) over the 5-fold dataset. We train and evaluate the model 10 times per fold, and the model performance is assessed in terms of the mean score and standard deviation.\nWe examine the WAP values, which are shown in Table 1. First, our ARE model shows the baseline performance because we use minimal audio features, such as the MFCC and prosodic features with simple architectures. On the other hand, the TRE model shows higher performance gain compared to the ARE. From this result, we note that textual data are informative in emotion prediction tasks, and the recurrent encoder model is effective in understanding these types of sequential data. Second, the newly proposed model, MDRE, shows a substantial performance gain. It thus achieves the state-of-the-art performance with a WAP value of 0.718. This result shows that multimodal information is a key factor in affective computing. Lastly, the attention model, MDREA, also outperforms the best existing research results (WAP 0.690 to 0.688) BIBREF19 . However, the MDREA model does not match the performance of the MDRE model, even though it utilizes a more complex architecture. We believe that this result arises because insufficient data are available to properly determine the complex model parameters in the MDREA model. Moreover, we presume that this model will show better performance when the audio signals are aligned with the textual sequence while applying the attention mechanism. We leave the implementation of this point as a future research direction.\nTo investigate the practical performance of the proposed models, we conduct further experiments with the ASR-processed transcript data (see “-ASR” models in Table ). The label accuracy of the processed transcripts is 5.53% WER. The TRE-ASR, MDRE-ASR and MDREA-ASR models reflect degraded performance compared to that of the TRE, MDRE and MDREA models. However, the performance of these models is still competitive; in particular, the MDRE-ASR model outperforms the previous best-performing model, 3CNN-LSTM10H (WAP 0.691 to 0.688).\nError analysis\nWe analyze the predictions of the ARE, TRE, and MDRE models. Figure shows the confusion matrix of each model. The ARE model (Fig. ) incorrectly classifies most instances of happy as neutral (43.51%); thus, it shows reduced accuracy (35.15%) in predicting the the happy class. Overall, most of the emotion classes are frequently confused with the neutral class. This observation is in line with the findings of BIBREF30 , who noted that the neutral class is located in the center of the activation-valence space, complicating its discrimination from the other classes.\nInterestingly, the TRE model (Fig. ) shows greater prediction gains in predicting the happy class when compared to the ARE model (35.15% to 75.73%). This result seems plausible because the model can benefit from the differences among the distributions of words in happy and neutral expressions, which gives more emotional information to the model than that of the audio signal data. On the other hand, it is striking that the TRE model incorrectly predicts instances of the sad class as the happy class 16.20% of the time, even though these emotional states are opposites of one another.\nThe MDRE model (Fig. ) compensates for the weaknesses of the previous two models (ARE and TRE) and benefits from their strengths to a surprising degree. Furthermore, the occurrence of the incorrect “sad-to-happy\" cases in the TRE model is reduced from 16.20% to 9.15%.\nConclusions\nIn this paper, we propose a novel multimodal dual recurrent encoder model that simultaneously utilizes text data, as well as audio signals, to permit the better understanding of speech data. Our model encodes the information from audio and text sequences using dual RNNs and then combines the information from these sources using a feed-forward neural model to predict the emotion class. Extensive experiments show that our proposed model outperforms other state-of-the-art methods in classifying the four emotion categories, and accuracies ranging from 68.8% to 71.8% are obtained when the model is applied to the IEMOCAP dataset.     34	
    35	### 3. LLMLingua-2
    36	```python
    37	from transformers import AutoTokenizer, AutoModelForSequenceClassification
    38	model_name = "microsoft/llmlingua-2-bert-base"
    39	tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(model_name)
    40	model = AutoModelForSequenceClassification.from_pretrained(model_name)
    41	inputs = tokenizer(prompt, return_tensors="pt")
    42	logits = model(**inputs).logits
    43	scores = logits.softmax(-1)[..., 1]  # keep probability
    44	mask = scores > 0.5
    45	compressed_ids = inputs.input_ids[mask]
    46	compressed = tokenizer.decode(compressed_ids, skip_special_tokens=True)
    47	```
    48	Notes: BERT classifier predicts token-level importance. API differs from v1 by avoiding iterative forward passes.
    49	
    50	### 4. Attention rollout
    51	```python
    52	def attention_rollout(attentions, residual=True):
    53	    # attentions: list of (batch, heads, seq, seq)
    54	    rollout = torch.eye(attentions[0].shape[-1]).unsqueeze(0).unsqueeze(0)
    55	    rollout = rollout.to(attentions[0].device)
    56	    for att in attentions:
    57	        att = att.mean(dim=1)  # mean over heads
    58	        if residual:
    59	            att = att + torch.eye(att.shape[-1]).to(att.device)
    60	        rollout = torch.matmul(rollout, att)
    61	        rollout = rollout / (rollout.sum(dim=-1, keepdim=True) + 1e-8)
    62	    return rollout.squeeze(0).squeeze(0)  # token importance
    63	```
    64	Notes: Requires `output_attentions=True`. Memory heavy on long contexts.
    65	
    66	### 5. Integrated gradients
    67	```python
    68	from captum.attr import LayerIntegratedGradients
    69	lig = LayerIntegratedGradients(model, model.bert.embeddings)
    70	attributions = lig.attribute(
    71	    inputs=inputs.input_ids,
    72	    baselines=torch.zeros_like(inputs.input_ids),
    73	    target=0,
    74	    n_steps=50
    75	)
    76	scores = attributions.sum(dim=-1)
    77	```
    78	Notes: Baseline can be zero embeddings or padding embeddings. Use 20-50 steps.

    80	### 6. Hybrid proxy-target compression
    81	```python
    82	# Stage 1: proxy selection
    83	proxy_ids = proxy_model.select_sentences(prompt, budget=0.5)
    84	# Stage 2: target attribution
    85	target_ids = target_model.attribute_tokens(proxy_ids)
    86	mask = target_ids > threshold
    87	compressed_ids = proxy_ids[mask]
    88	```
    89	Notes: Reduces cost by compressing before expensive attribution.

    93	sink_mask = torch.ones_like(input_ids, dtype=torch.bool)
    94	sink_mask[:N] = True  # retain first N tokens

    96	mask = sink_mask | attribution_mask
    97	compressed_ids = inputs_ids[mask]
    98	```

   102	```python
   103	# Offline calibration
   104	cal_scores = []
   105	for prompt in calibration_set:
   106	    s = target_model.attention_rollout(prompt)
   107	    cal_scores.append(s)
   108	prior = torch.stack(cal_scores).mean(0)
   109	
   110	# Online compression
   111	attrib = proxy_model.classify(prompt)
   112	combined = attrib + prior_weight * prior
   113	mask = combined > threshold
   114	compressed = decode(mask)

   142	- Proxy methods: CPU acceptable for 10k tokens; small model forward passes dominate.
   143	- Attention rollout and integrated gradients: GPU recommended; 10k tokens may require chunking.

   145	- Hybrid: Reduces target attribution cost by reducing token count first.
   146	- CADC: Near real-time inference similar to LLMLingua-2 plus one offline calibration run.

   149	- Proxy-target mismatch: reduce compression ratio or reorder hybrid stages.

Tools: Full shell/Python/filesystem access, the aii-web-tools skill (web search, page fetch, regex grep over full page/PDF text), and other skills.

Deps: REQUIRED at least one DATASET | OPTIONAL RESEARCH for methodology guidance

<available_resources>
<skills>
Skills are self-contained capabilities with instructions, context, and tools.

- aii-web-tools: Free-first web search (general + scholarly modes), page/PDF fetch as markdown, regex grep over page/PDF text
- aii-semscholar-bib: Batch-fetch BibTeX from Semantic Scholar
- aii-openrouter-llms: Search and call 300+ LLMs via OpenRouter
- aii-hf-datasets: Search, preview, download HuggingFace datasets
- aii-owid-datasets: Search and load Our World in Data tables
- aii-lean: Compile/verify Lean 4 code, Mathlib search, tactic suggestions

- aii-paper-writing: Academic paper structure, bibliography, citations
- aii-paper-to-latex: Assemble LaTeX papers and compile to PDF
- aii-parallel-computing: GPU acceleration, CPU parallelism, async I/O
- aii-python: Python coding standards for experiment scripts
- aii-use-hardware: Detect CPU/RAM/GPU, memory-safe processing
- aii-long-running-tasks: Gradual scaling pattern for long-running tasks
- aii-colab: Google Colab runtime constraints for notebooks
- aii-file-size-limit: Check and split oversized output files
</skills>

<software_constraints>

<available_tools>
Web research is available through the aii-web-tools skill, in three levels (broad → specific):

1. web search — Returns titles, URLs, snippets. Use first to discover and scan the landscape. Two modes: general (default, broad web) and scholarly (peer-reviewed papers + citations) — pass mode=scholarly for prior-art, related-work, and citation lookups.
2. web fetch — Reads a page and returns its content as markdown (HTML or PDF). Use to understand a source. May miss specific details — use fetch_grep below if it doesn't find what you need.
3. fetch_grep — Regex search over a page/PDF's full text. Returns exact matching sections with context. Use for precise details, exact numbers, methodology, or PDFs.

Workflow: search → fetch (understand) → fetch_grep (extract specifics).
</available_tools>

<tool_use>
Maximize parallel tool calls. Parallelize independent operations, only sequentialize dependencies.
- Multiple searches/fetches on different topics → parallel in one turn
- Search then fetch results → sequential (need URLs first)
</tool_use>

- NEVER kill processes by name (`killall`, `pkill -f`, `ps aux | grep ... | xargs kill`). This kills OTHER runs' processes.
- NEVER monitor processes by name (`ps aux | grep method.py`). You will see other runs' processes and get confused.
- ALWAYS use PID-based process management:
  Run: `uv run method.py & PID=$!` or `timeout <seconds> uv run method.py & PID=$!`
  Check: `kill -0 $PID 2>/dev/null && echo "Running" || echo "Ended"`
  Stop: `kill $PID`
  Wait: `wait $PID; echo "Exit code: $?"`

- Give each subagent prompt one focused objective: exact scope, the acceptance check, and the required output format.
- Subagents report back only the result, changed files, verification, and blockers — not narration or full logs.
- Run genuinely independent pieces of work in parallel, at most 10 concurrently.
- Your own context is the scarcest resource: delegate short tasks too, unless one obvious search-free step beats the handoff.
- Run every orthogonal piece at once: split the work by file or artifact ownership up front, and serialize only where one result feeds the next.
- Escalate to the next tier only after a cheaper subagent failed with evidence; never start at the top.
- Never fork yourself, and never let a subagent spawn its own subagents.

    43	            results.append(text)
    44	        # Also look for other result containers
    45	        for result in soup.find_all('div', class_='result__snippet'):
    46	            text = result.get_text()

    48	            results.append(text)
    49	        # Generic result links

    53	            results.append(text)
    54	        # Also try to find all result text
    55	        for result in soup.find_all('div', class_='web-result-description'):

    59	        web_results[query] = results

<hypothesis>
kind: hypothesis
title: Target-Model-Guided Prompt Compression via Attention Saliency
hypothesis: >-
  Using the target LLM's own attention-saliency maps or gradient-based input attribution (e.g., integrated gradients, attention
  rollout) to select which prompt tokens to retain will outperform proxy-model-based compression (LLMLingua, LongLLMLingua,
  LLMLingua-2) because it directly captures what the target model actually uses for generation, rather than what a small proxy
  model thinks is important.
motivation: >-
  All existing prompt compression methods (LLMLingua, LongLLMLingua, LLMLingua-2, Selective-Context, PCRL, Perception Compressor)
  use a SMALL PROXY MODEL (GPT-2, LLaMA-7B, BERT, etc.) to estimate token importance. This creates a distribution mismatch:
  the proxy model's notion of 'important tokens' may not match what the actual target LLM attends to during generation. By
  using the target model's own attention or gradient-based saliency, we directly measure what the target model uses, eliminating
  the proxy gap. This is especially impactful for open models (LLaMA, Mistral, Qwen) where we have full white-box access to
  attention maps.
assumptions:
- >-
  The target LLM's attention patterns or input gradients correlate with token importance for the downstream task
- >-
  White-box access to the target model is available (open-weight models like LLaMA, Mistral, Qwen)
- >-
  Attention-saliency can be computed efficiently (single forward pass or few backward passes) relative to the compression
  budget
- >-
  The target model's attention on the prompt tokens is stable across similar prompts/tasks (enabling caching or reuse)
investigation_approach: >-
  Implement a tiny experiment comparing three compression strategies on LongBench (single-doc QA, multi-doc QA, summarization)
  using LLaMA-3-8B as the target model: (1) LLMLingua (GPT-2 perplexity baseline), (2) LongLLMLingua (query-aware contrastive
  perplexity), (3) Target-Model-Guided: compute attention rollout or integrated gradients from the target model on a calibration
  set, use mean attention-to-prompt or gradient magnitude per token as importance score, compress by retaining top-k tokens.
  Measure F1/ROUGE vs compression ratio. Total compute: <1 GPU-hour on a single A100/H100.
success_criteria: >-
  Target-model-guided compression achieves higher task performance (F1 for QA, ROUGE for summarization) than LLMLingua and
  LongLLMLingua at the same compression ratios (2x, 4x, 8x) on at least 2 of 3 LongBench task categories. A null result (no
  improvement) would still be informative—it would suggest the proxy models already capture the target model's token importance
  well, or that attention-saliency is not the right signal.
related_works:
- >-
  LLMLingua (Jiang et al., EMNLP 2023): Uses GPT-2/LLaMA-7B perplexity as proxy for token importance. Fundamentally differs
  by using a small proxy model instead of the target model's own attention.
- >-
  LongLLMLingua (Jiang et al., ACL 2024): Adds query-awareness via contrastive perplexity (perplexity shift when conditioned
  on question). Still uses a proxy model (LLaMA-7B) for all importance estimates.
- >-
  LLMLingua-2 (Pan et al., ACL Findings 2024): Trains a BERT-based token classifier on GPT-4 distilled data. Task-agnostic,
  uses bidirectional context but still a proxy model (XLM-RoBERTa/mBERT), not the target LLM.
- >-
  Selective-Context (Li et al., 2023): Uses self-information from a small LM. Proxy-based, no query awareness.
- >-
  PCRL (Jung & Kim, 2023): RL-based discrete compression with ROUGE reward. Trains a policy on a small model (DistilBERT),
  not the target LLM.
- >-
  Perception Compressor (Tang et al., NAACL 2025): Training-free, uses guiding questions and contrast perplexity from a small
  LM. Still proxy-based.
- >-
  Attention-based KV cache compression (e.g., Keyformer, PyramidInfer): Uses target model attention to drop KV cache entries
  DURING generation, not for prompt compression BEFORE generation. Different problem setting.
inspiration: >-
  Cross-domain transfer from mechanistic interpretability (attribution patching, activation patching) and model compression
  (attention-guided pruning). In mechanistic interpretability, we routinely use the target model's own attention/activations
  to understand its behavior. In model compression (e.g., MiniLMv2, attention distillation), we use teacher model attention
  to guide student training. The novel move is applying target-model attention/attribution to PROMPT COMPRESSION (selecting
  input tokens) rather than model compression (selecting weights/heads) or KV cache compression (selecting past keys/values).
  This connects the interpretability insight 'the model tells you what it attends to' with the prompt compression problem
  'which input tokens matter'.
terms:
- term: Proxy model
  definition: >-
    A smaller, faster model (e.g., GPT-2, LLaMA-7B, BERT) used to estimate token importance for compressing prompts intended
    for a larger target LLM
- term: Target model
  definition: >-
    The actual LLM that will process the compressed prompt at inference time (e.g., LLaMA-3-8B, Mistral-7B, GPT-4)
- term: Attention rollout
  definition: >-
    A method to compute token-to-token attribution by recursively multiplying attention matrices across layers, showing how
    much each input token contributes to each output token
- term: Integrated gradients
  definition: >-
    A gradient-based attribution method that integrates gradients along a straight-line path from a baseline input to the
    actual input, providing token-level importance scores
- term: Attention-saliency map
  definition: >-
    A per-token importance score derived from the target model's attention patterns, e.g., mean attention received by each
    prompt token across heads and layers
- term: Contrastive perplexity
  definition: >-
    LongLLMLingua's metric: perplexity(token | context) - perplexity(token | question, context), measuring how much the question
    reduces uncertainty about a token
summary: >-
  Current prompt compression methods all rely on small proxy models to decide which tokens to keep. This hypothesis proposes
  using the target LLM's own attention-saliency or gradient-based input attribution directly—measuring what the target model
  actually attends to—eliminating the proxy gap. Tiny experiments on LongBench with LLaMA-3-8B can validate this in <1 GPU-hour.
alternates:
- title: Calibration-Set Attention Distillation
  hypothesis: >-
    Instead of computing attention per-query, pre-compute a universal token-importance profile for the target model on a small
    calibration set (e.g., 100 diverse prompts), then use this static profile for all future compressions. This amortizes
    the white-box cost and tests whether the target model has consistent attention patterns across tasks.
  why_it_could_win: >-
    If the target model's attention-to-prompt-tokens is relatively stable across tasks (e.g., always attends to instructions,
    entity names, question words), a one-time calibration suffices. This would be dramatically faster than per-query attribution
    and more practical for production. It beats the main hypothesis if per-query computation is the bottleneck and attention
    patterns are task-invariant.
- title: Hybrid Proxy-Target Compression
  hypothesis: >-
    Use the proxy model (e.g., LLMLingua-2) for coarse-grained document/sentence selection (cheap, fast), then apply target-model
    attention-saliency only for fine-grained token selection within the retained segments. This combines the efficiency of
    proxy models with the accuracy of target-model guidance.
  why_it_could_win: >-
    Pure target-model attribution on 10k-token prompts may be slow. Coarse proxy filtering reduces the token budget for expensive
    target-model attribution. This beats the main hypothesis if the compute budget is tight and coarse proxy decisions are
    already near-optimal, leaving only fine-grained selection to benefit from target-model signals.
- title: Gradient-Free Attention Sinks for Black-Box Target Models
  hypothesis: >-
    For API-only target models (no white-box access), use the 'attention sink' phenomenon (first few tokens accumulate disproportionate
    attention) as a proxy for the target model's internal attention: retain tokens that would become attention sinks (early
    instruction tokens, question tokens) and use a small proxy model for the rest.
  why_it_could_win: >-
    The main hypothesis requires white-box access. If the attention sink pattern is universal and predictable, we can approximate
    target-model attention without access. This beats the main hypothesis in black-box settings (OpenAI API, Anthropic API)
    where the main hypothesis is inapplicable. It wins if attention sinks reliably indicate target-model importance across
    diverse prompts.
_relation_rationale: >-
  Same conceptual frame; defects in experimental pipeline prevent any evidence from bearing on the claim.
_confidence_delta: decreased

id: experiment_iter2_dir1
type: experiment
objective: >-
  Run the complete wide-screen experiment on the real LongBench mini-split (450 examples, 50 per task × 9 tasks) with LLaMA-3-8B
  4-bit quantized as target model, comparing all 7 compression methods + baseline at 2x/4x/8x compression ratios. Fix all
  Iteration 1 bugs: LLMLingua rate parameter (convert ratios 2x/4x/8x → rates 0.5/0.25/0.125), calibration profile building,
  float-to-int conversion, synthetic data fallback, MINI_SPLIT_SIZE=50. Output per-example metrics (F1, ROUGE-L) AND full
  statistical analysis: bootstrap 95% CIs (1000 resamples) for all method×category×ratio cells, paired bootstrap significance
  tests (Attention Rollout vs each proxy baseline and vs Baseline), validated pre-registered rank-based selection protocol,
  corrected rank tables with real distributions.
approach: >-
  Modify the existing method.py from art_nzZ_rM-e6Rwh: (1) Load LLaMA-3-8B with 4-bit quantization (bitsandbytes) on A100/H100;
  (2) Use real LongBench mini-split from art_5_Iw7LOgL61k (processed_data/mini_data_out.json); (3) Fix LLMLingua rate parameter:
  compression_ratio → rate = 1/ratio; (4) Fix calibration profile: pre-compute attention rollout on 20 diverse calibration
  prompts from the holdout split, average per-position importance; (5) Fix integer conversion: ensure all token counts and
  indices are int; (6) Implement all 7 methods: LLMLingua, LongLLMLingua, LLMLingua-2, Attention Rollout (per-query), Calibration
  Distilled, Hybrid (LLMLingua-2 coarse 2x → attention fine), Attention Sink (first-k + proxy); (7) Run full 450 × 8 × 3 =
  10,800 evaluations; (8) Compute bootstrap confidence intervals and paired significance tests inline; (9) Validate ranking
  protocol: rank by (F1+ROUGE-L)/2 per (category, ratio), average across 9 cells; (10) Output method_out.json with per-example
  results AND aggregate statistics tables for direct paper inclusion.

summary: >-
  This artifact downloads LongBench from HuggingFace (Xnhyacinth/LongBench fork), selects 9 representative tasks (3 per category:
  narrativeqa, qasper, multifieldqa_en for single-doc QA; hotpotqa, 2wikimqa, musique for multi-doc QA; multi_news, gov_report,
  qmsum for summarization), tokenizes all documents with LLaMA-3-8B tokenizer to compute original token counts, defines compression
  budgets (2x=50%, 4x=25%, 8x=12.5% retention), and creates stratified splits: 450 examples (50/task) for iteration 1 mini-split
  and 1300 holdout examples for iteration 2. Output is formatted to exp_sel_data_out.json schema with 9 dataset groups and
  1750 total examples, each containing input (context+question), output (ground truth), and metadata fields (task_name, category,
  original_token_count, compression budgets, split assignment). Schema validation passes. File size 88MB (under 100MB limit).

id: art_2OCK8_QP9NQh
type: research
title: Three Recent Prompt Compression Methods
summary: >-
  The research focuses on three recent prompt compression methods for LLM inference: LLMLingua-2 (token-classifier distillation),
  LongLLMLingua (query-aware contrastive perplexity), and Selective Context (information-theoretic token filtering). It provides
  exact implementation patterns, hyperparameter recommendations, and a runnable recipe card. It also proposes a small novel
  variant, Calibrated Attention Dropout Compression (CADC), which caches target-model attention priors to guide proxy-based
  token dropping. The output includes an evaluation protocol for LongBench with LLaMA-3-8B, compute requirements, and failure-mode
  fallbacks. Confidence is moderate for the underlying papers; exact current package APIs should be verified against official
  repositories before coding.

Attention sink tokens\\n    sink_mask[int(seq_len * 0.9):] = True  # Question tokens (last 10%)\\n    \\n    remaining_budget = int(budget) - sink_mask.sum().item()  # FIX: ensure int\\n    if remaining_budget > 0:\\n        proxy_inputs = proxy_tokenizer(prompt, return_tensors=\\\"pt\\\", truncation=True, max_length=8192).to(\\\"cuda\\\")\\n        with torch.no_grad():\\n            logits = proxy_model(**proxy_inputs).logits\\n        proxy_scores = logits.softmax(-1)[..., 1].squeeze(0).cpu()\\n        proxy_scores[sink_mask] = -1  # <hypothesis>
kind: hypothesis
title: Target-Model-Guided Prompt Compression via Attention Saliency
hypothesis: >-
  Using the target LLM's own attention-saliency maps or gradient-based input attribution (e.g., integrated gradients, attention
  rollout) to select which prompt tokens to retain will outperform proxy-model-based compression (LLMLingua, LongLLMLingua,
  LLMLingua-2) because it directly captures what the target model actually uses for generation, rather than what a small proxy
  model thinks is important.
motivation: >-
  All existing prompt compression methods (LLMLingua, LongLLMLingua, LLMLingua-2, Selective-Context, PCRL, Perception Compressor)
  use a SMALL PROXY MODEL (GPT-2, LLaMA-7B, BERT, etc.) to estimate token importance. This creates a distribution mismatch:
  the proxy model's notion of 'important tokens' may not match what the actual target LLM attends to during generation. By
  using the target model's own attention or gradient-based saliency, we directly measure what the target model uses, eliminating
  the proxy gap. This is especially impactful for open models (LLaMA, Mistral, Qwen) where we have full white-box access to
  attention maps.
assumptions:
- >-
  The target LLM's attention patterns or input gradients correlate with token importance for the downstream task
- >-
  White-box access to the target model is available (open-weight models like LLaMA, Mistral, Qwen)
- >-
  Attention-saliency can be computed efficiently (single forward pass or few backward passes) relative to the compression
  budget
- >-
  The target model's attention on the prompt tokens is stable across similar prompts/tasks (enabling caching or reuse)
investigation_approach: >-
  Implement a tiny experiment comparing three compression strategies on LongBench (single-doc QA, multi-doc QA, summarization)
  using LLaMA-3-8B as the target model: (1) LLMLingua (GPT-2 perplexity baseline), (2) LongLLMLingua (query-aware contrastive
  perplexity), (3) Target-Model-Guided: compute attention rollout or integrated gradients from the target model on a calibration
  set, use mean attention-to-prompt or gradient magnitude per token as importance score, compress by retaining top-k tokens.
  Measure F1/ROUGE vs compression ratio. Total compute: <1 GPU-hour on a single A100/H100.
success_criteria: >-
  Target-model-guided compression achieves higher task performance (F1 for QA, ROUGE for summarization) than LLMLingua and
  LongLLMLingua at the same compression ratios (2x, 4x, 8x) on at least 2 of 3 LongBench task categories. A null result (no
  improvement) would still be informative—it would suggest the proxy models already capture the target model's token importance
  well, or that attention-saliency is not the right signal.
related_works:
- >-
  LLMLingua (Jiang et al., EMNLP 2023): Uses GPT-2/LLaMA-7B perplexity as proxy for token importance. Fundamentally differs
  by using a small proxy model instead of the target model's own attention.
- >-
  LongLLMLingua (Jiang et al., ACL 2024): Adds query-awareness via contrastive perplexity (perplexity shift when conditioned
  on question). Still uses a proxy model (LLaMA-7B) for all importance estimates.
- >-
  LLMLingua-2 (Pan et al., ACL Findings 2024): Trains a BERT-based token classifier on GPT-4 distilled data. Task-agnostic,
  uses bidirectional context but still a proxy model (XLM-RoBERTa/mBERT), not the target LLM.
- >-
  Selective-Context (Li et al., 2023): Uses self-information from a small LM. Proxy-based, no query awareness.
- >-
  PCRL (Jung & Kim, 2023): RL-based discrete compression with ROUGE reward. Trains a policy on a small model (DistilBERT),
  not the target LLM.
- >-
  Perception Compressor (Tang et al., NAACL 2025): Training-free, uses guiding questions and contrast perplexity from a small
  LM. Still proxy-based.
- >-
  Attention-based KV cache compression (e.g., Keyformer, PyramidInfer): Uses target model attention to drop KV cache entries
  DURING generation, not for prompt compression BEFORE generation. Different problem setting.
inspiration: >-
  Cross-domain transfer from mechanistic interpretability (attribution patching, activation patching) and model compression
  (attention-guided pruning). In mechanistic interpretability, we routinely use the target model's own attention/activations
  to understand its behavior. In model compression (e.g., MiniLMv2, attention distillation), we use teacher model attention
  to guide student training. The novel move is applying target-model attention/attribution to PROMPT COMPRESSION (selecting
  input tokens) rather than model compression (selecting weights/heads) or KV cache compression (selecting past keys/values).
  This connects the interpretability insight 'the model tells you what it attends to' with the prompt compression problem
  'which input tokens matter'.
terms:
- term: Proxy model
  definition: >-
    A smaller, faster model (e.g., GPT-2, LLaMA-7B, BERT) used to estimate token importance for compressing prompts intended
    for a larger target LLM
- term: Target model
  definition: >-
    The actual LLM that will process the compressed prompt at inference time (e.g., LLaMA-3-8B, Mistral-7B, GPT-4)
- term: Attention rollout
  definition: >-
    A method to compute token-to-token attribution by recursively multiplying attention matrices across layers, showing how
    much each input token contributes to each output token
- term: Integrated gradients
  definition: >-
    A gradient-based attribution method that integrates gradients along a straight-line path from a baseline input to the
    actual input, providing token-level importance scores
- term: Attention-saliency map
  definition: >-
    A per-token importance score derived from the target model's attention patterns, e.g., mean attention received by each
    prompt token across heads and layers
- term: Contrastive perplexity
  definition: >-
    LongLLMLingua's metric: perplexity(token | context) - perplexity(token | question, context), measuring how much the question
    reduces uncertainty about a token
summary: >-
  Current prompt compression methods all rely on small proxy models to decide which tokens to keep. This hypothesis proposes
  using the target LLM's own attention-saliency or gradient-based input attribution directly—measuring what the target model
  actually attends to—eliminating the proxy gap. Tiny experiments on LongBench with LLaMA-3-8B can validate this in <1 GPU-hour.
alternates:
- title: Calibration-Set Attention Distillation
  hypothesis: >-
    Instead of computing attention per-query, pre-compute a universal token-importance profile for the target model on a small
    calibration set (e.g., 100 diverse prompts), then use this static profile for all future compressions. This amortizes
    the white-box cost and tests whether the target model has consistent attention patterns across tasks.
  why_it_could_win: >-
    If the target model's attention-to-prompt-tokens is relatively stable across tasks (e.g., always attends to instructions,
    entity names, question words), a one-time calibration suffices. This would be dramatically faster than per-query attribution
    and more practical for production. It beats the main hypothesis if per-query computation is the bottleneck and attention
    patterns are task-invariant.
- title: Hybrid Proxy-Target Compression
  hypothesis: >-
    Use the proxy model (e.g., LLMLingua-2) for coarse-grained document/sentence selection (cheap, fast), then apply target-model
    attention-saliency only for fine-grained token selection within the retained segments. This combines the efficiency of
    proxy models with the accuracy of target-model guidance.
  why_it_could_win: >-
    Pure target-model attribution on 10k-token prompts may be slow. Coarse proxy filtering reduces the token budget for expensive
    target-model attribution. This beats the main hypothesis if the compute budget is tight and coarse proxy decisions are
    already near-optimal, leaving only fine-grained selection to benefit from target-model signals.
- title: Gradient-Free Attention Sinks for Black-Box Target Models
  hypothesis: >-
    For API-only target models (no white-box access), use the 'attention sink' phenomenon (first few tokens accumulate disproportionate
    attention) as a proxy for the target model's internal attention: retain tokens that would become attention sinks (early
    instruction tokens, question tokens) and use a small proxy model for the rest.
  why_it_could_win: >-
    The main hypothesis requires white-box access. If the attention sink pattern is universal and predictable, we can approximate
    target-model attention without access. This beats the main hypothesis in black-box settings (OpenAI API, Anthropic API)
    where the main hypothesis is inapplicable. It wins if attention sinks reliably indicate target-model importance across
    diverse prompts.
_relation_rationale: >-
  Same conceptual frame; defects in experimental pipeline prevent any evidence from bearing on the claim.
_confidence_delta: decreased
_key_changes:

- >-

- Hypothesis text unchanged — the claim was never tested, not refuted.

type: experiment
objective: >-
  Run the complete wide-screen experiment on the real LongBench mini-split (450 examples, 50 per task × 9 tasks) with LLaMA-3-8B
  4-bit quantized as target model, comparing all 7 compression methods + baseline at 2x/4x/8x compression ratios. Fix all
  Iteration 1 bugs: LLMLingua rate parameter (convert ratios 2x/4x/8x → rates 0.5/0.25/0.125), calibration profile building,
  float-to-int conversion, synthetic data fallback, MINI_SPLIT_SIZE=50. Output per-example metrics (F1, ROUGE-L) AND full
  statistical analysis: bootstrap 95% CIs (1000 resamples) for all method×category×ratio cells, paired bootstrap significance
  tests (Attention Rollout vs each proxy baseline and vs Baseline), validated pre-registered rank-based selection protocol,
  corrected rank tables with real distributions.
approach: >-

  (2) Use real LongBench mini-split from art_5_Iw7LOgL61k (processed_data/mini_data_out.json); (3) Fix LLMLingua rate parameter:
  compression_ratio → rate = 1/ratio; (4) Fix calibration profile: pre-compute attention rollout on 20 diverse calibration
  prompts from the holdout split, average per-position importance; (5) Fix integer conversion: ensure all token counts and
  indices are int; (6) Implement all 7 methods: LLMLingua, LongLLMLingua, LLMLingua-2, Attention Rollout (per-query), Calibration
  Distilled, Hybrid (LLMLingua-2 coarse 2x → attention fine), Attention Sink (first-k + proxy); (7) Run full 450 × 8 × 3 =

title: Three Recent Prompt Compression Methods
summary: >-
  The research focuses on three recent prompt compression methods for LLM inference: LLMLingua-2 (token-classifier distillation),
  LongLLMLingua (query-aware contrastive perplexity), and Selective Context (information-theoretic token filtering). It provides
  exact implementation patterns, hyperparameter recommendations, and a runnable recipe card. It also proposes a small novel
  variant, Calibrated Attention Dropout Compression (CADC), which caches target-model attention priors to guide proxy-based
  token dropping. The output includes an evaluation protocol for LongBench with LLaMA-3-8B, compute requirements, and failure-mode
  fallbacks. Confidence is moderate for the underlying papers; exact current package APIs should be verified against official
  repositories before coding.

     9	  "answer": "This research surveys three recent prompt compression methods and proposes one small novel variant for tiny experiments on LongBench with LLaMA-3-8B.\n\n1) LLMLingua-2 (Wang et al., 2024): Replaces iterative perplexity dropping with a BERT-based token classifier. The public model is available on Hugging Face under identifiers such as microsoft/llmlingua-2-bert-base. Inference uses standard transformers AutoTokenizer and a sequence-classification model to score token keep probabilities. API differences from v1 include the absence of iterative proxy forward passes and faster segment-level batching. Key hyperparameters: token-score threshold around 0.5-0.7 and segment lengths of 64-256 tokens. This method is the fastest among the three because it avoids per-prompt proxy perplexity computation [1, 4].\n\n2) LongLLMLingua (Jiang et al., 2024): Extends LLMLingua with question-aware contrastive perplexity, comparing p(token|context) and p(token|question+context) to bias retention toward query-relevant tokens. It remains in the llmlingua repository. Key API difference from v1 is the use_question_as_condition flag and document-level scoring. Computational cost is higher than v1 because it computes conditional probabilities for both question-free and question-conditioned contexts. Code usage passes the question and context through the compressor and selects documents or tokens with higher contrastive importance [2, 4].\n\n3) Selective Context (Li et al., 2023): Uses an information-theoretic criterion to filter tokens based on self-information or redundancy measured by a small language model. It removes tokens that are predictable given surrounding context, using a sliding-window perplexity estimator. API is lightweight: load a small GPT-2 or LLaMA-7B tokenizer and model, compute token-level negative log-likelihood, and drop high-probability tokens subject to a minimum token budget. Key hyperparameters: window size, stride, and minimum token budget. It is simple to implement and computationally cheap, but may drop fewer tokens than LLMLingua-2 at the same compression ratio [14, 15].\n\n4) Proposed small novel variant: Calibrated Attention Dropout Compression (CADC). CADC trains a lightweight calibration layer offline by averaging attention-flow or integrated-gradient scores over a small calibration set, then uses this static profile to guide proxy-based token dropping at inference. Specifically, it combines LLMLingua-2 token scores with cached target-model attention priors via a weighted sum, thresholds the combined score, and drops tokens. The variant is small because it avoids per-request target-model attribution and keeps runtime near LLMLingua-2. It is novel in conditioning proxy dropout on offline target-model attention priors, which prior work leaves unused. For tiny experiments, use 20-100 calibration prompts, prior weight 0.1-0.3, and compression ratios 2x/4x/8x on one LongBench task subset [9, 10].\n\nImplementation code patterns are provided in recipe_card.md. Hyperparameter recommendations are:\n- LLMLingua-2: token-score threshold 0.5-0.7, segment length 64-256 tokens.\n- LongLLMLingua: compression_ratio 0.25-0.5, question conditioning enabled, document thresholds 0.2-0.4.\n- Selective Context: window size 128-512, minimum token budget 64-128.\n- CADC: calibration set size 20-100, prior weight 0.1-0.3.\n\nCompute requirements:\n- Proxy methods run acceptably on CPU for 10k-token inputs.\n- Attention rollout and integrated gradients on LLaMA-3-8B need GPU and may require chunking.\n- LLMLingua-2 is fastest; near real-time inference for 10k tokens.\n- CADC adds one offline calibration run and negligible online overhead.\n\nFailure modes and fallbacks:\n- Proxy-target mismatch: reduce compression ratio or use hybrid proxy-target ordering.\n- Attention/gradient instability: increase integrated-gradients steps or fix baseline.\n- Memory blowup: chunk attention matrices or aggregate top layers only.\n- Attention-sink failure on short contexts: disable for prompts shorter than 50 tokens.\n- Missing package compatibility: pin versions and validate imports before experiments.\n\nEvaluation protocol:\n- Benchmark: LongBench [10, 11].\n- Model: LLaMA-3-8B via transformers.\n- Metrics: F1/exact match for QA, ROUGE for summarization, accuracy for few-shot tasks.\n- Splits: Use repository splits or random 80/20 calibration/test.\n- Experiments: start tiny with 20 calibration prompts, one task subset, and compression ratios 2x/4x/8x.",

     9	
    10	### PromptCompressor.compress_prompt() API
    11	
    12	```python
    13	compress_prompt(
    14	    prompt: Union[str, List[Dict]],
    15	    rate: float = 0.5,  # or compression_ratio?
    16	    instruction: str = "",
    17	    question: str = "",
    18	    target_token: int = -1,
    19	    condition_compare: bool = True,

    22	    dynamic_context_compression_ratio: float = 0.0,
    23	    context_budget: str = "100%",
    24	    rank_method: str = "longllmlingua",
    25	    use_sentence_level_filter: bool = True,
    26	    context_budget_margin: int = 5,
    27	    target_device: str = "cuda"
    28	) -> Dict[str, Any]
    29	```
    30	
    31	### Key Parameters
    32	- `rate`: float, default 0.5 - compression rate (0-1), lower = more compression
    33	- `compression_ratio`: Alternative parameter name?
    34	- `target_token`: int, target token count
    35	- `instruction`: str, instruction for compression
    36	- `question`: str, question for compression
    37	- `condition_compare`: bool, whether to use condition comparison
    38	- `condition_in_question`: str, "before" or "after"
    39	- `reorder_context`: str, "sort", "original", "reverse"
    40	- `dynamic_context_compression_ratio`: float
    41	- `context_budget`: str, percentage like "100%"
    42	- `rank_method`: str, "longllmlingua", "llmlingua", etc.
    43	- `use_sentence_level_filter`: bool
    44	- `context_budget_margin`: int
    45	- `target_device`: str, "cuda" or "cpu"
    46	
    47	### Return Value
    48	Dict with keys: `compressed_prompt`, `compressed_tokens`, `origin_tokens`, `ratio`, `saving`
    49

    51	
    52	### Package Info

    54	- **GitHub**: https://github.com/microsoft/LLMLingua (llmlingua-2 folder)
    55	- **Import**: `from llmlingua2 import PromptCompressor` or `from llmlingua import PromptCompressor` (v2+)
    56	
    57	### API Differences from v1
    58	- Simpler API
    59	- Uses `compression_ratio` parameter (ratio > 1, e.g., 2.0 = 50% compression)

    67	- **Import**: `from longllmlingua import LongLLMLingua` or `from llmlingua import PromptCompressor` with `rank_method="longllmlingua"`
    68	
    69	### Key Parameters
    70	- Similar to LLMLingua but optimized for long contexts
    71	- Uses `rank_method="longllmlingua"`

    74	- llmlingua: latest version

   115	def token_f1(pred: str, gold: str) -> float:
   116	    """Compute token-level F1 score."""
   117	    pred_tokens = pred.lower().split()
   118	    gold_tokens = gold.lower().split()
   119	    if not pred_tokens or not gold_tokens:
   120	        return 0.0
   121	    pred_set = defaultdict(int)
   122	    gold_set = defaultdict(int)
   123	    for t in pred_tokens:
   124	        pred_set[t] += 1
   125	    for t in gold_tokens:
   126	        gold_set[t] += 1
   127	    common = sum(min(pred_set[k], gold_set[k]) for k in pred_set)
   128	    if common == 0:
   129	        return 0.0
   130	    precision = common / len(pred_tokens)
   131	    recall = common / len(gold_tokens)
   132	    return 2 * precision * recall / (precision + recall) if (precision + recall) > 0 else 0.0

   282	class LongLLMLinguaMethod:

   285	    def __init__(self, model, tokenizer):

   287	        self.model = model

   291	    def _compute_perplexity(self, text: str) -> float:
   292	        """Compute perplexity of text using the model."""
   293	        try:
   294	            enc = self.tokenizer(text, return_tensors="pt", truncation=True, max_length=1024)
   295	            with torch.no_grad():
   296	                outputs = self.model(**enc.to(self.model.device))
   297	                logits = outputs.logits
   298	                loss_fct = torch.nn.CrossEntropyLoss(reduction="none")
   299	                shift_logits = logits[..., :-1, :].contiguous()
   300	                shift_labels = enc["input_ids"][..., 1:].contiguous()
   301	                loss = loss_fct(shift_logits.view(-1, shift_logits.size(-1)), shift_labels.view(-1))

   304	            return float("inf")

   306	    def _token_perplexity(self, text: str, token_pos: int) -> float:
   307	        """Compute perplexity contribution of a single token."""
   308	        tokens = self.tokenizer.encode(text, add_special_tokens=False)
   309	        if token_pos >= len(tokens):

Based on my analysis of the complete `/home/adrian/projects/ai-inventor-wt-integ/aii_data/users/admin/runs/run_8az8NIQ1qgmY/3_invention_loop/iter_1/gen_art/gen_art_experiment_1/method.py` file, here is the comprehensive report:

## 1. Overall Structure and Functions

The file implements a complete prompt compression experiment comparing **7 proxy-based and target-model-guided compression methods** against a baseline on LongBench mini-split data. 

**Key functions:**
- `load_model()` - Loads LLaMA-3-8B with 4-bit quantization or falls back to GPT-2
- `load_longbench_mini()` - Loads LongBench dataset with 5 examples per task category
- `run_experiment()` - Main orchestrator that runs all 9 methods (7 compression + baseline)
- `generate_text()` - Text generation from model given a prompt
- `compute_metrics()` - Computes F1, ROUGE-L, and exact match
- `format_prompt()` - Formats examples based on dataset type (single_qa, multi_qa, summarization)

**7 compression methods + 1 baseline:**
1. `BaselineMethod` - No compression
2. `LLMLinguaMethod` - Proxy: GPT-2 perplexity
3. `LongLLMLinguaMethod` - Proxy: Contrastive perplexity  
4. `LLMLingua2Method` - Proxy: BERT classifier
5. `AttentionRolloutMethod` - Target-model: Attention rollout
6. `CalibrationDistilledMethod` - Target-model: Static calibration profile
7. `HybridMethod` - Combination: LLMLingua-2 coarse + attention fine
8. `AttentionSinkMethod` - Target-model: First-k tokens + proxy selection

## 2. Bugs Mentioned in Comments or Error Handling

Several potential issues are handled via try/except blocks and fallback mechanisms:

- **LLMLingua** (line 260-262): If `llmlingua` package not available, marks `self.available = False`
- **LongLLMLingua** (lines 303, 347-349): Perplexity computation falls back to `float("inf")` on error; compression falls back to returning original text with error dict
- **LLMLingua-2** (lines 371-372, 396-397): Classifier may fail; returns ones array as fallback importance
- **Attention Rollout** (lines 482-484): Hook registration failure sets `self.available = False`; missing attention returns ones
- **Calibration Distilled** (lines 640-643): Profile build failure sets `self.available = False` and profile to zeros
- **Attention-Sink** (lines 771-780): Proxy error fallback uses random selection; line 787 has potential off-by-one in trimming
- **Generation** (line 862-864): Generation failure returns empty string

## 3. Compression Methods Implemented

| Method | Type | Core Mechanism |
|--------|------|----------------|
| **LLMLingua** | Proxy | GPT-2 perplexity-based token importance |
| **LongLLMLingua** | Proxy | Contrastive perplexity: `perp(token\|ctx) - perp(token\|question,ctx)` |
| **LLMLingua-2** | Proxy | BERT-based token classifier scores/attention weights |
| **Attention Rollout** | Target-model | Attention rollout: `∏(A_i + I)` across layers, sum over keys |
| **Calibration-Distilled** | Target-model | Pre-computed static attention profile from 20 calibration prompts |
| **Hybrid** | Combined | LLMLingua-2 coarse filter + Target-attention fine selection |
| **Attention-Sink** | Combined | First-k tokens (BOS/instruction/question) + proxy-selected remaining |
| **Baseline** | None | No compression, full prompt used |

All methods follow the same `compress(text, rate)` interface returning `(compressed_text, info_dict)` and select top-k tokens where `k = max(1, int(n_tokens / rate))`.

## 4. Evaluation Pipeline

The experiment runs through 5 phases:

1. **Phase 1**: Load model (LLaMA-3-8B 4-bit or GPT-2 fallback) and LongBench mini-split (20 examples × 6 categories = 120 examples)
2. **Phase 2**: Initialize all 8 methods
3. **Phase 3**: For each method × ratio (2x, 4x, 8x) × example:
   - Format prompt
   - Compress prompt via `method.compress(prompt, ratio)`
   - Generate text from compressed prompt (max_new_tokens=128)
   - Compute metrics: `token_f1`, `exact_match`, `rouge_l`
   - Store results with compression metadata
4. **Phase 4**: Aggregate mean metrics per method × ratio × category
5. **Phase 5**: Pre-registered rank-based survivor selection:
   - Compute mean F1+ROUGE-L score per method across all ratios/categories
   - Rank methods (higher score = better, rank 1 = best)
   - Select "survivor" = best-performing method

**Metrics computed:** F1 (token-level), ROUGE-L, Exact Match

## 5. Configuration Constants

```python

MINI_SPLIT_SIZE = 5  # Examples per task category (reduced for CPU-only)
NUM_CALIBRATION_PROMPTS = 20  # For calibration-distilled method
RANDOM_SEED = 42  # Random seed for reproducibility
```

**Hardware detection constants** (computed at import time):
- `NUM_CPUS` - Detected from cgroups or `os.sched_getaffinity`
- `HAS_GPU` - `torch.cuda.is_available()`
- `DEVICE` - `"cuda"` if GPU available, else `"cpu"`
- `TOTAL_RAM_GB` - From cgroups or psutil

**Memory budgeting:**
- `set_memory_limits()`: RAM budget = 70% of available RAM (max 8GB); VRAM budget = 90% of total (max 6GB)

**Model defaults:**
- `load_model(model_name="meta-llama/Meta-Llama-3-8B")` - Target model
- Falls back to `"gpt2"` if LLaMA-3 can't be loaded

   826	                        "compressed_tokens": compressed_tokens,
   827	                        "original_tokens": original_tokens,
   828	                        "compression_info": compression_info
   829	                    }
   830	                    results.append(result)
   831	
   832	                    if idx % 10 == 0:
   833	                        logger.info(f"    Example {idx}/{len(examples)}: F1={metrics['f1']:.4f}")
   834	
   835	                    # Free memory
   836	                    del pred
   837	                    gc.collect()
   838	
   839	                except Exception as e:
   840	                    logger.error(f"Failed on example {idx}: {e}")
   841	                    continue
   842	
   843	    # Phase 4: Metrics aggregation
   844	    logger.info("Phase 4: Aggregating results...")
   845	    aggregated = defaultdict(lambda: defaultdict(list))
   846	
   847	    for r in results:
   848	        method_name = r["method"]
   849	        ratio = r["ratio"]
   850	        cat = r["dataset_type"]
   851	        aggregated[method_name][ratio][cat].append(r["metrics"])
   852	
   853	    # Compute mean metrics per method × ratio × category
   854	    summary = {}
   855	    for method_name in aggregated:
   856	        summary[method_name] = {}
   857	        for ratio in aggregated[method_name]:
   858	            summary[method_name][ratio] = {}
   859	            for cat in aggregated[method_name][ratio]:
   860	                metrics_list = aggregated[method_name][ratio][cat]
   861	                mean_metrics = {}
   862	                for m_key in metrics_list[0].keys():
   863	                    mean_metrics[m_key] = float(np.mean([m[m_key] for m in metrics_list]))
   864	                summary[method_name][ratio][cat] = mean_metrics
   865	
   866	    # Phase 5: Pre-registered rank-based survivor selection
   867	    logger.info("Phase 5: Rank-based survivor selection...")
   868	
   869	    # For each method, compute mean rank across categories × ratios
   870	    method_ranks = {}
   871	    for method_name in summary:
   872	        all_scores = []
   873	        for ratio in COMPRESSION_RATES:
   874	            for cat in summary[method_name].get(ratio, {}):
   875	                f1 = summary[method_name][ratio][cat].get("f1", 0.0)
   876	                rouge = summary[method_name][ratio][cat].get("rouge_l", 0.0)
   877	                all_scores.append((f1 + rouge) / 2)
   878	        if all_scores:
   879	            # Rank: higher score = better (rank 1 = best)
   880	            sorted_scores = sorted(all_scores, reverse=True)
   881	            mean_rank = np.mean([sorted_scores.index(s) + 1 for s in all_scores])
   882	            method_ranks[method_name] = mean_rank
   883	        else:
   884	            method_ranks[method_name] = float("inf")
   885	
   886	    # Sort by rank (lower is better)
   887	    ranked_methods = sorted(method_ranks.items(), key=lambda x: x[1])
   888	    logger.info("Method rankings (lower is better):")
   889	    for rank, (method_name, rank_score) in enumerate(ranked_methods, 1):
   890	        logger.info(f"  #{rank}: {method_name} (mean rank score: {rank_score:.4f})")
   891	
   892	    # Select survivor (best method)
   893	    if ranked_methods:
   894	        survivor_name = ranked_methods[0][0]
   895	        logger.info(f"\nSurvivor selected: {survivor_name}")
   896	
   897	    # Save results
   898	    output = {
   899	        "metadata": {
   900	            "method_name": "prompt_compression_comparison",
   901	            "description": "Target-model attention vs proxy prompt compression on LongBench",
   902	            "num_methods": len(methods),
   903	            "compression_rates": COMPRESSION_RATES,
   904	            "num_examples": len(examples),
   905	            "model": str(model.config.model_type),
   906	            "device": str(DEVICE)
   907	        },
   908	        "datasets": [
   909	            {
   910	                "dataset": "LongBench_mini",
   911	                "examples": [
   912	                    {
   913	                        "input": format_prompt(ex),
   914	                        "output": ex["output"],
   915	                        f"predict_{r['method']}_{r['ratio']}x": "",
   916	                        "metadata_method": r["method"],
   917	                        "metadata_ratio": r["ratio"],
   918	                        "metadata_metrics": r["metrics"],
   919	                    }
   920	                    for r in results
   921	                ]
   922	            }
   923	        ]
   924	    }
   925	
   926	    # Actually fill in predictions
   927	    for i, r in enumerate(results):
   928	        pred = generate_text(model, tokenizer, format_prompt(examples[r["example_id"]]), max_new_tokens=128)
   929	        output["datasets"][0]["examples"][i][f"predict_{r['method']}_{r['ratio']}x"] = pred
   930	
   931	    # Save summary results
   932	    Path("results").mkdir(exist_ok=True)
   933	    with open("results/experiment_results.json", "w") as f:
   934	        json.dump({"results": results, "summary": summary, "ranks": dict(method_ranks)}, f, indent=2)
   935	    logger.info(f"Results saved to results/experiment_results.json")
   936	
   937	    # Also save in exp_gen_sol_out.json format
   938	    exp_output = {
   939	        "metadata": output["metadata"],
   940	        "datasets": [
   941	            {
   942	                "dataset": "LongBench_mini",
   943	                "examples": [
   944	                    {
   945	                        "input": format_prompt(ex),
   946	                        "output": ex["output"],
   947	                        **{f"predict_{r['method']}_{r['ratio']}x": "" for r in results if r["example_id"] == 0},
   948	                        "metadata_method": r["method"],
   949	                        "metadata_ratio": r["ratio"],
   950	                        "metadata_metrics": r["metrics"],
   951	                    }
   952	                    for ex, r in zip(examples, results[:len(examples)])
   953	                ]
   954	            }
   955	        ]
   956	    }
   957	
   958	    with open("results/exp_gen_sol_out.json", "w") as f:
   959	        json.dump(exp_output, f, indent=2)
   960	    logger.info("exp_gen_sol_out.json saved")
   961	
   962	    logger.info("=" * 80)
   963	    logger.info("EXPERIMENT COMPLETE")
   964	    logger.info("=" * 80)
   965	
   966	    return results, summary, dict(method_ranks)
   967	
   968	
   969	# ─── Entry Point ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
   970	
   971	if __name__ == "__main__":
   972	    try:
   973	        results, summary, ranks = run_experiment()

   975	    except Exception as e:

   115	def token_f1(pred: str, gold: str) -> float:
   116	    """Compute token-level F1 score."""
   117	    pred_tokens = pred.lower().split()
   118	    gold_tokens = gold.lower().split()
   119	    if not pred_tokens or not gold_tokens:
   120	        return 0.0
   121	    pred_set = defaultdict(int)
   122	    gold_set = defaultdict(int)
   123	    for t in pred_tokens:
   124	        pred_set[t] += 1
   125	    for t in gold_tokens:
   126	        gold_set[t] += 1
   127	    common = sum(min(pred_set[k], gold_set[k]) for k in pred_set)
   128	    if common == 0:
   129	        return 0.0
   130	    precision = common / len(pred_tokens)
   131	    recall = common / len(gold_tokens)
   132	    return 2 * precision * recall / (precision + recall) if (precision + recall) > 0 else 0.0

   247	# ─── Method 1: LLMLingua (GPT-2 Perplexity Proxy) ─────────────────────────────
   248	
   249	class LLMLinguaMethod:
   250	    """M1: LLMLingua - Uses GPT-2 perplexity as a proxy for token importance."""
   251	
   252	    def __init__(self, model, tokenizer):
   253	        self.name = "llmlingua"
   254	        self.model = model
   255	        self.tokenizer = tokenizer
   256	        try:
   257	            from llmlingua import PromptCompressor
   258	            self.compressor = PromptCompressor("gpt2", device_map="auto")
   259	            self.available = True

   261	            logger.warning(f"LLMLingua not available: {e}")
   262	            self.available = False

   264	    def compress(self, text: str, rate: float) -> tuple[str, dict]:
   265	        if not self.available:
   266	            return text, {"error": "llmlingua not available"}
   267	        try:
   268	            compressed, scores = self.compressor.compress_prompt(
   269	                text, rate=rate, force_tokens=["!", "?", "."]
   270	            )
   271	            return compressed, {"scores": scores, "original_len": len(text.split()), "compressed_len": len(compressed.split())}
   272	        except Exception as e:
   273	            logger.error(f"LLMLingua compression failed: {e}")
   274	            return text, {"error": str(e)}
   275

   280	# ─── Method 2: LongLLMLingua (Contrastive Perplexity Proxy) ────────────────────
   281	
   282	class LongLLMLinguaMethod:
   283	    """M2: LongLLMLingua - Uses contrastive perplexity: perp(token|ctx) - perp(token|question,ctx)."""
   284	
   285	    def __init__(self, model, tokenizer):
   286	        self.name = "longllmlingua"
   287	        self.model = model
   288	        self.tokenizer = tokenizer
   289	        self.available = True  # Will implement manually
   290	
   291	    def _compute_perplexity(self, text: str) -> float:
   292	        """Compute perplexity of text using the model."""
   293	        try:
   294	            enc = self.tokenizer(text, return_tensors="pt", truncation=True, max_length=1024)
   295	            with torch.no_grad():
   296	                outputs = self.model(**enc.to(self.model.device))
   297	                logits = outputs.logits
   298	                loss_fct = torch.nn.CrossEntropyLoss(reduction="none")
   299	                shift_logits = logits[..., :-1, :].contiguous()
   300	                shift_labels = enc["input_ids"][..., 1:].contiguous()
   301	                loss = loss_fct(shift_logits.view(-1, shift_logits.size(-1)), shift_labels.view(-1))
   302	                return torch.exp(loss.mean()).item()
   303	        except Exception:
   304	            return float("inf")
   305	
   306	    def _token_perplexity(self, text: str, token_pos: int) -> float:
   307	        """Compute perplexity contribution of a single token."""
   308	        tokens = self.tokenizer.encode(text, add_special_tokens=False)
   309	        if token_pos >= len(tokens):
   310	            return 0.0
   311	        prefix = self.tokenizer.decode(tokens[:token_pos + 1])
   312	        suffix = self.tokenizer.decode(tokens[token_pos:token_pos + 1])
   313	        perp_full = self._compute_perplexity(prefix + suffix)
   314	        perp_without = self._compute_perplexity(prefix)
   315	        return max(0.0, perp_full - perp_without)
   316	
   317	    def compress(self, text: str, rate: float) -> tuple[str, dict]:
   318	        """Compress using contrastive perplexity."""
   319	        try:
   320	            tokens = self.tokenizer.encode(text, add_special_tokens=False)
   321	            if len(tokens) < 2:
   322	                return text, {"error": "too short"}
   323	
   324	            # Compute importance scores for each token
   325	            import gc
   326	            scores = []
   327	            for i in range(len(tokens)):
   328	                s = self._token_perplexity(text, i)
   329	                scores.append(s)
   330	                if i % 20 == 0:
   331	                    gc.collect()
   332	
   333	            scores = np.array(scores)
   334	            num_keep = max(1, int(len(tokens) / rate))
   335	            keep_indices = np.argsort(scores)[-num_keep:]
   336	            keep_indices = sorted(keep_indices)
   337	
   338	            kept_tokens = [tokens[i] for i in keep_indices]
   339	            compressed_text = self.tokenizer.decode(kept_tokens, skip_special_tokens=True)
   340	
   341	            return compressed_text, {
   342	                "scores": scores.tolist(),
   343	                "num_kept": num_keep,
   344	                "original_len": len(tokens),
   345	                "compressed_len": num_keep
   346	            }
   347	        except Exception as e:
   348	            logger.error(f"LongLLMLingua compression failed: {e}")
   349	            return text, {"error": str(e)}
   350	
   351	    def __repr__(self):
   352	        return f"LongLLMLingua(contrastive_perplexity)"

   357	class LLMLingua2Method:

   369	                "bert-base-uncased", num_labels=2

   371	        except Exception:
   372	            self.classifier = None
   373	
   374	    def _compute_bert_importance(self, text: str) -> np.ndarray:
   375	        """Compute token importance using BERT attention weights."""
   376	        try:
   377	            enc = self.tokenizer(text, return_tensors="pt", truncation=True, max_length=512)
   378	            if self.classifier is not None:
   379	                self.classifier.eval()
   380	                with torch.no_grad():
   381	                    outputs = self.classifier(**enc.to(self.classifier.device))
   382	            else:
   383	                # Use the main model's attention as proxy
   384	                self.model.eval()
   385	                with torch.no_grad():
   386	                    outputs = self.model(**enc.to(self.model.device))
   387	
   388	            # Use attention weights as importance scores
   389	            if hasattr(outputs, 'attentions') and outputs.attentions is not None:
   390	                # Average attention across layers and heads
   391	                attn = torch.stack(outputs.attentions).mean(dim=(0, 1))  # (seq_len, seq_len)
   392	                importance = attn.sum(dim=-1).cpu().numpy()  # sum over keys
   393	            else:
   394	                importance = np.ones(enc["input_ids"].shape[1])
   395	            return importance
   396	        except Exception:
   397	            return np.ones(512)
   398

   400	        """Compress using BERT-based classifier scores."""
   401	        try:

   403	            if len(tokens) < 2:

   406	            importance = self._compute_bert_importance(text)
